prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose and poetry that build an expansive metaphysical architecture out of memory, the body and dream

statement.case_for: I keep Cărtărescu first after reading my colleagues' openings. The case rests on voice, formal ambition and imaginative depth. Blinding and Solenoid, as I understand them from public knowledge and the longlist description, treat memory, the body and dream as one metaphysical project, and they do so in a voice that is hard to confuse with anyone else's. The project is built on a large scale and seems to deepen across decades rather than repeat. The novels sit on a foundation of poetry, and they draw on both the Romanian tradition and the European fantastic and modernist lineages. Several colleagues describe the achievement in similar terms, but I weigh it on those literary grounds and not on how many members rank him first. A citation can be scoped cleanly to a single writer: visionary prose with poetry as a supporting strand.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation concerns sustained quality and what I can actually judge. Very long, recursive and self-referential books may be uneven across their length, and I cannot assess that from the descriptions or from translation. The density and rhythm of Romanian prose reach me only through translations whose fidelity I cannot verify. My knowledge of the poetry and early fiction is partial, so the 'whole oeuvre' judgment rests mostly on the late novels. Adonis offers a clearer and more historically documented formal and linguistic achievement, since he renewed the possibilities of Arabic verse itself. If the committee gives priority to that kind of transformation of a literary language, my ordering could reasonably be questioned.

responses.point: Olsson places Adonis first for a sustained, decades-long remaking of Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and dialogue with tradition, and he sees no concern about timing or depth. He ranks Cărtărescu fourth and notes that the later volumes are very long and may not hold up evenly.
responses.response: I agree that Adonis's formal and linguistic achievement is of the first rank, and I ranked him second for that reason. His case also depends on prosody, allusion and interplay with classical forms that I and most readers meet only through translation. I cannot say that this uncertainty is smaller than the one for Cărtărescu. The point about the length and evenness of Solenoid is fair, and I cannot resolve it from the evidence supplied. I do think that a prose project built from large-scale structure, recurring images and an overall architecture is somewhat less exposed to translation loss than verse that depends on prosodic effects. That is a judgment, not something I have verified. So I disagree on the order but not on Adonis's standing, and I keep him as my first alternative.

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson first for an unmistakable voice, a sustained reconfiguration of genre, and exceptional intellectual depth. She notes that the citation scope must stay with Carson's own writing and describe book-objects carefully.
responses.response: I accept the voice and the formal inventiveness. I ranked Carson third and keep her as an alternative. I agree with Sward's scoping: the citation should not rest on the translations and scholarship. My hesitation is about the whole body of work. Some of her best-known pieces depend on book design, layout or performance, and that makes it harder to be sure the whole oeuvre has the same sustained depth as the best books. Cărtărescu's project, by comparison, is more continuously one architecture of prose. I recognize that this is a difference of kind, and a committee that values genre-crossing renewal could weigh it differently.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for voice, imaginative scale and an architecture that holds across volumes. She ranks Carson second but asks whether the whole body of work reaches the sustained depth the will asks for or whether some of it is better seen as brilliant formal experiment.
responses.response: I share both parts of this. I agree that Cărtărescu's strength is voice and imaginative scale, and I also share her uncertainty about how the poetry and early work compare with the later novels. Her question about Carson, whether the work is sustained depth or formal experiment, is the same reservation I have, and it is a real reason I place Carson below Cărtărescu and Adonis. I would add that Mattson's concern about translation of the Romanian prose applies equally to Adonis. Neither first-place case can claim an advantage on that point.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and describes a coherent, escalating project and sustained quality. He places Magris fifth, questions whether Magris's voice has the formal intensity of the strongest contenders, and weighs the essayistic hybrid against purely imaginative fiction.
responses.response: I agree with the substance of the Cărtărescu case and with the caution about Magris. I ranked Magris fifth because of his erudition, the historical imagination in the hybrid form, and the coherence of his Central European subject. I do not think his formal intensity matches the leading candidates', and the balance between essay and fiction is unresolved. So I would not move him ahead of the three candidates I put first. A mind trained in non-fiction might be drawn to him, but my own non-fiction background is context here and not evidence for any candidate.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's density, rhythm and wordplay survives translation from Romanian is unknown, and I cannot verify translation quality.
My coverage of his poetry and early fiction is partial, so the whole-oeuvre judgment rests mainly on the late novels.
I cannot tell whether the very long late books sustain quality evenly across their length.
I have not independently verified any source and rely on public knowledge and the supplied longlist descriptions.
Whether the Adonis case, resting on Arabic prosody that I cannot assess in the original, deserves more weight than my translation-based reading allows is unresolved.
Whether a co-opted member votes in the committee is undocumented. My simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile that requires recusal. The profile shows no personal, professional or archival tie to any shortlisted writer. It records only collegial or biographical connections that do not involve the candidates: she was elected to the Academy alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg in 2020, she is married to former finance minister Pär Nuder, and her Nobel biography drew on Nobel Foundation archives. I do not treat these as bearing on any shortlisted candidate.
